teach.title: The person who gets it
teach.say: When someone gives, hands, says or answers something, there are two people in play: the thing given is the object, and the person on the receiving end goes into **the dative (the 'to/for' form)**, *cāsus datīvus*. *Iūlius servō nummum dat* = Julius gives the slave a coin. No preposition is used, and no word order marks it — only the ending. The question word is *cui?* (to whom?).

teach.title: A servus-type receiver ends in -ō
teach.say: A receiver whose dictionary form ends in -us (*servus*, *dominus*, *fīlius*) ends **-ō** in the dative singular: *servō*, *dominō*, *fīliō*. Names in -us do it too: *Mārcō*, *Quīntō*. A word in -um takes the very same ending (*oppidum* → *oppidō*), though a thing is seldom the one receiving. It is the same -ō as the ablative, so the sentence, not the ending, tells you which it is.

teach.title: An ancilla-type receiver ends in -ae
teach.say: A receiver whose dictionary form ends in -a (*fīlia*, *puella*, *ancilla*, and the name *Syra*) ends **-ae** in the dative singular: *fīliae*, *puellae*, *Syrae*. Say it as two sounds, ah-ee, and remember that it is the giving-to ending, whatever else -ae may also be.

teach.title: More than one receiver: -īs
teach.say: Two or more receivers take the dative plural, and both families end **-īs**: *servīs*, *puerīs*, *puellīs*. Nothing else changes — the thing given stays in the object form, and the verb still agrees with the subject, not with the receivers.

teach.title: The pater family: -ī and -ibus
teach.say: Nouns whose genitive ends in -is (*pater, patris*; *māter, mātris*) build the dative on that stem: **-ī** in the singular, **-ibus** in the plural — *patrī*, *mātrī*, *patribus*, *mātribus*. The job is exactly the same; only the two endings are new.

teach.title: Two words in -ae: which one receives?
teach.say: *fīliae* can be the dative (the receiver, to the daughter) or the genitive (the owner, of the daughter), and *dominī* can be the genitive too. Work from the verb: the giving verb needs exactly one receiver, and any other case-mate hangs on a noun. *Mārcus fīliae dominī rosam dat* = Marcus gives a rose to the master's daughter — *fīliae* receives, *dominī* owns.

core.text: When someone gives, says or shows something, the person on the receiving end goes into **the dative (the 'to/for' form)**, *cāsus datīvus*: *Iūlius Mārcō mālum dat* = Julius gives Marcus an apple, gives an apple to Marcus. The thing given stays in the accusative (the object form); the receiver takes -ō, -ae, -ī in the singular and -īs, -ibus in the plural. The question word is *cui?* (to whom?). No preposition, ever.
The indirect object is the person something is given to: *he gave her a flower* — *her* receives, *a flower* is what is given. English can also say *to her*; Latin says it with the ending.
Verbs of giving, telling and showing (*dat*, *dīcit*, *ostendit*, *mōnstrat*) put the receiver in the dative: -ae / -ō / -ī singular, -īs / -ibus plural.

invented.en: The teacher tells the pupils a story.

core.text: In the plural the dative and the ablative are twins: *servīs*, *puellīs*, *ovibus*. Ask what the word is doing. A person who receives is dative: *servīs māla dat* — gives the slaves apples. A thing something is done with is ablative: *baculō verberat*. Living receiver, dative; tool, ablative.

more.text: From the learner's notes: 'dative' means the giving case, because giving verbs so often need an indirect object — someone the verb touches only at second hand. English places it before the direct object or adds *to* / *for*; Latin never uses word order or a preposition for it. The notes' chart adds the is-nouns: dative -ī, plural -ibus (*Vir ūvās fēminae dat*, *fīliō*, *fīliīs*).

Ørberg cap. VII: datīvus -ō / -īs, -ae / -īs, and neuter *oppidō* (*fluvius oppidō aquam dat*); pronouns *eī*, *iīs*, later *mihi*, *tibi*. Two look-alikes: the singular dative of a-nouns equals the genitive (*puellae*), and of us-nouns equals the ablative (*servō*); the verb settles it. The dative also marks the person something is for or who is affected (*hominī necesse est* — it is necessary for a person, r10:58.1; *mihi placet* — it pleases me), and goes with a few verbs that take no object (*pāret* — obeys: *ancilla pāret*, r07:19.1). A&G §361–367.
